intro: Five long reads for a slow week: what is left for mathematicians once machines prove the theorems, why China has not locked up its AI as American forecasters expected, how the Victorian elite turned parties into statecraft, why America is losing its feel for the long future, and what AI means for India's back-office boom.

stories.headline: When the machine proves it, who understands?
stories.dek: Quanta's mathematics editor argues that AI's theorem-proving has broken the field's reward system, and that mathematicians must now decide what their work is for.
body: Through the summer of 2026, artificial-intelligence systems turned out proofs of conjectures that had stood for decades. So when OpenAI announced on September 8th that its models had solved one of mathematics' most famous problems (Quanta's own news report called it one of the million-dollar Millennium Prize Problems), the result was not wholly a surprise. It still landed, writes Jordana Cepelewicz, the magazine's mathematics editor, as something abrupt. A dispute over authorship and standards followed.

Scott Aaronson, a computer scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, wrote on his blog that he no longer expects to prove theorems in the years left to him, because he is no longer needed for it. Human mathematicians, he said, have lost their place as the main theorem-provers on Earth.

Cepelewicz's essay is not a report on the proof. It tries to explain why a result that outsiders greet as plainly good news has shaken those inside the field. Her answer is that most people misunderstand what mathematics is for, and that the discipline's own reward system has made much the same mistake.
## A long afternoon at Berkeley

Two days after the announcement, about 150 students, postdoctoral researchers and professors gathered at Berkeley to hear Ken Ono, a mathematician on leave from the University of Virginia to work at Axiom Math, an AI startup. He told them that their profession might change beyond recognition or cease to exist, and that they needed to brace.

The room did not take it quietly. Questions interrupted him throughout. One student criticised the way AI companies were treating mathematics. When Ono said that mathematicians would do their very best, another asked what that effort actually amounted to. A talk scheduled for 50 minutes ran beyond two hours, and students stayed afterwards to vent and to console one another.
## Teleported to the summit

Pure mathematics, in Cepelewicz's telling, sits somewhere between the sciences and the arts. Marcel Goh, a doctoral student at McGill, calls it either the most scientific of the humanities or the most humanistic of the sciences.

Problems are often chosen for the journey they promise: the tools invented along the way, the unexpected links between distant fields, the detours. The value, Goh says, was never the theorems alone. It lay in carrying on a tradition of deep reasoning and shared knowledge that has no market price.

Machine-made proofs skip all that. Their logic is checked by formal verification systems, so mathematicians know they are correct. But they are hard to read, the essay reports. They leave out key steps, dwell on irrelevancies, and do not say how they connect to the existing literature. Cepelewicz offers an image: it is like being set down on a mountain peak in fog, without the route, the equipment or the companions that a climb would have supplied. One has the answer and little else.
## A broken equilibrium

Why does this feel like a threat and not a gift? Because the culture of mathematics has long treated proving a theorem as the evidence of understanding. Doctorates, publications, jobs and prizes are all counted in theorems proved. Tasmin Chu of Caltech says AI breaks the system by pushing it to its extreme. Daniel Litt of the University of Toronto says the existing equilibrium has broken and a new one must be found.

The essay lists strains that are already visible. Companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic now compete with mathematicians, and sometimes hire them, while publishing few clear explanatory papers. OpenAI has said it is keeping more than 100 important results secret, which discourages researchers from working on questions that may already be settled. Chu calls this a huge damage to open science, done in the service of shareholders. Some mathematicians have stopped stating open conjectures in their papers for fear that models will scrape them.

Journals and the arXiv preprint server are flooded with AI-generated or AI-assisted proofs that nobody can easily check, and arXiv now limits authors to two submissions a month. An editor at Transactions on Machine Learning Research contacted the authors of ten papers headed for rejection and found that most either did not reply or could not answer basic questions about work they claimed as their own. Activity on MathOverflow, the field's question-and-answer forum, is falling sharply as students put their questions to models in private.
## Two futures

Litt sketches the bleak version. Students are trained to press buttons without reading what comes out, and within 50 years mathematics withers. He does not think this likely, but he thinks it is roughly where doing nothing leads. Matilde Marcolli of Caltech, writing in the London Mathematical Society's newsletter, warns that treating conjectures as the only goal and the only reward could end the profession. The danger she sees is a loss of imagination, not of mathematics as such.

The hopeful version comes from Pavel Etingof of MIT. If machines do the hard labour of discovery, humans can turn to interpreting and understanding what has been found, and there will be plenty of such work to do. A theorem proved by AI, he argues, becomes part of mathematical culture only once people have read and understood it. Litt hopes machine proofs will one day arrive as elegant expositions. Cepelewicz invokes Roland Barthes's 1967 essay "The Death of the Author", which held that readers make a text's meaning. Future mathematicians, she suggests, may be readers of that kind.
## The vegetarians

Whether anyone will want that job is less clear. People go into pure mathematics, Chu observes, to author creative work and to have it appreciated by a community. A conversation in which machines talk and humans listen is less appealing.

Goh describes the present culture as sick and feels pressure to use AI simply to keep up. He and some others have taken to calling themselves AI "vegetarians", restricting their use of it. He says he would sooner leave the field than use AI in creative work, though he means to stay as long as he can.

There is collective action too. Mathematicians are rethinking how they train students and whom they hire, and journals are experimenting with requiring a talk to accompany an accepted paper. Chu and colleagues have founded an Association for Human Mathematics, on the argument that what the field most needs now is policy proposals and tools, not more mathematics.

Cepelewicz is candid about the limits of her case. Skills such as understanding, communication and vision are harder to measure than a count of theorems, though she expects progress. She is less certain that new generations will be drawn to a remade discipline. Inertia is powerful, and the field had other troubles, inequity and limited access among them, before any of this began.

Her conclusion is conditional. Adaptation will be hard, but a mathematics that rewards exposition, breadth, experiment and deep thought over the publication of theorem after theorem might be stronger for it. Litt imagines a lively community of people doing the most interesting work of their lives. And if the field fails to adapt, he asks, whose fault would that be?
stories.counterpoint: A sceptic would say the essay mourns a guild more than a science. Settled theorems are a public good whoever proves them, and the complaints about unreadable proofs describe today's models, not necessarily next year's. If machines learn to write clear expositions, as Litt himself hopes, the interpreter's role may be automated in turn, leaving the hopeful scenario no more secure than the old one. The piece also draws mainly on the worried, and offers little evidence of how widely the mood is shared.
stories.why: Mathematics is the first scholarly field in which machines appear to be overtaking experts at the very task by which those experts are judged. How it rebuilds its incentives once results are cheap is a preview for every profession that measures people by outputs a model can produce. The difference between having an answer and understanding it will matter well beyond mathematics.
questions: In your own work, which outputs are rewarded as stand-ins for understanding, and what would be left if a machine produced them?
Is a proof that nobody understands knowledge? If so, whose?
If you were hiring a young mathematician in 2030, what would you ask to see?

source.title: Is AI the End of Math As We Know It?
source.author: Jordana Cepelewicz

stories.headline: The awakening in Beijing that never came
stories.dek: Farrell Gregory argues that American forecasters expected China to lock up its AI because they assumed everyone reasons as they do.
body: The day before Xi Jinping addressed the World AI Conference in July 2026, Moonshot AI, a Chinese laboratory, released its Kimi K3 model with open weights. Xi's speech then called for openness, open source and sharing. For many American technologists this was the wrong script. They had expected Beijing, as frontier systems grew costlier and more dangerous, to pull its models back behind closed doors.

Farrell Gregory, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, uses that mismatch as the starting point for a long essay in Palladium. His claim is that the people who built America's mental model of the AI race, many of them shaped by Bay Area rationalism, assumed that China would see the technology as they do and act accordingly. It has not, and he thinks the error is philosophical before it is strategic.

Gregory gives the forecasters their due. Leopold Aschenbrenner's "Situational Awareness", published in the summer of 2024, was right to doubt that America's lead was secure. "AI 2027", from the AI Futures Project, was read in the White House and correctly foresaw a rapid build-out and autonomous agents. But both leaned on a moment of Chinese awakening that has yet to arrive.
## What the documents say

The essay first reads China's own policy papers, which Gregory describes as slogan-heavy and measured. The 2017 Next Generation AI Development Plan set a goal of world leadership by 2030, framed around industrial competitiveness. At a Politburo study session in 2018 Xi called for China to hold the high ground in core technologies. A second session in 2025, the first on AI in seven years, stressed technical self-sufficiency.

American papers sound different. The year before, a congressional commission had called for a Manhattan Project-like programme for artificial general intelligence. America's 2025 AI Action Plan framed the field as a winner-take-all race. Gregory summarises the American strategy as a race to scale large language models towards superintelligence. China's "AI+" plan, by contrast, mentions neither competition nor America. It dwells on diffusion, standards and economic applications.
He cautions that such documents should not necessarily be taken at face value. But he asks why the Chinese narrative simply ignores the race.
## Openness under supervision

Part of the answer, he suggests, is that China already has the tools to keep open models on a leash. Generative models must be registered and reviewed before deployment, with continuing tests by provincial and central offices of the Cyberspace Administration of China. The regulator mainly licenses algorithms but can order changes. A campaign in 2026 led Alibaba, Zhipu, MiniMax and DeepSeek to act against malicious code and cyber threats, though Gregory warns that much of the reporting on such enforcement comes from state media.
This apparatus, part of what he calls a broader cybersecurity state, may allow China to sustain wide access to capable open models where Americans assume a hard choice between openness and safety.
## The limits of a universal calculus

The essay's central section is a critique of rationalism. Gregory traces the movement through the blogs Overcoming Bias, LessWrong and Slate Star Codex, notes that it was discussing AI risk long before GPT-3, and credits its vocabulary and its people with outsized influence at the leading labs. Its weakness, in his account, is an assumption that different polities will have similar utility functions when faced with a transformative technology.

He places this in an older American habit. Drawing on Richard Madsen's "China and the American Dream", he describes a line running from missionaries to market reformers, each expecting China to converge on American norms. "AI 2027" imagined China's leader nationalising frontier research in mid-2026. The authors have since acknowledged that their "China Wakes Up" moment has not happened, and that they would probably have heard if the party had consolidated the country's AI projects. Gregory says the assumptions need revising, not just the dates.

For a better frame he turns to Yuk Hui, a philosopher of technology, who separates tendencies, the universal principles of a technology, from facts, its contingent local features. Neural networks are a tendency shared by Silicon Valley and Beijing. Attitudes to existential risk, to job loss and to cyberattack are facts, and they vary by place.
## The economics of giving it away

Open weights are also a commercial weapon. Gregory argues that cheap Chinese models erode the moat around American frontier labs. He cites SemiAnalysis reporting that Anthropic's inference margins rose from 38% to 70%, and notes that Anthropic plans a public offering this year with OpenAI expected to follow in 2027, both having raised money at valuations near $1trn. A long spell of price compression, he argues, would hurt them badly.

Chinese labs, meanwhile, are learning to stay open and still earn. Kimi K3's licence requires outside businesses earning more than $20m a year from the model to negotiate commercial terms. DeepSeek cut the cost of its V4 model by 75% earlier in 2026. In a leaked investor call in May its founder, Liang Wenfeng, said prices were set for a reasonable profit and not maximum income, and predicted that its frontier models would stay open. An Economist analysis cited in the essay reckons Chinese firms will spend about a tenth of what American firms do on the build-out.
## Whose jobs are exposed

Gregory adds a structural reason for divergence. Kai-Fu Lee argued in 2018, building on Hans Moravec's observation that adult cognitive tasks are easier to automate than a toddler's physical ones, that AI would reach American office workers before it reached Chinese factory hands. In the figures Gregory gives, 23% of Chinese workers were in agriculture and 29% in manufacturing and industry in 2023. In America in 2025, 43% were in management and professional occupations and 18% in sales and office work. The same technology threatens different people.

The contrast showed in September 2026. After an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned with a public warning of catastrophic risk, the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI endorsed an open letter on "pacing the frontier". On September 12th China's minister of state security, Chen Yixin, published an article on AI's risks. It covered disinformation, cyberattacks, data leaks and military uses, and criticised monopoly and closed ecosystems. It did not mention job losses or safety in the American sense.
## Hypotheses, not prophecy

Gregory is careful about what he has shown. His explanations are, in his words, just hypotheses. Chen may be bound by the party line, though Gregory calls that reading unfalsifiable. The difference may turn out to be only one of timing, and Beijing may change course as capabilities grow. He suggests Chinese leaders may resist a slowdown because they already live under American chip controls imposed in 2022, or because their regulators make independent evaluators seem unnecessary.

His conclusion is that rationalist method remains valuable for reasoning under uncertainty but fails when it presumes shared goals. Outsiders should read Chinese media and debate closely, and Chinese officials might also imagine the future more freely.
stories.counterpoint: Gregory's own caveat may be the whole story: two years of divergence is thin evidence against a prediction about what states do once systems become truly dangerous. Open weights suit a challenger that is behind, and Beijing's incentives could flip the moment its labs lead. Reading official documents and a security minister's article as a window on Chinese thinking has the weakness he admits, since what is not said may simply be what cannot be said. And the forecasters he criticises did get the pace of the technology broadly right.
stories.why: Much of America's AI policy, from chip controls to talk of pacing the frontier, rests on a guess about how China will behave. If that guess assumed shared fears, then both the safety case for a lead and the business case for closed models are weaker than they look. The essay is also a useful general warning about mistaking one's own priorities for a universal calculus.
questions: Which of your beliefs about how a rival will act are really beliefs about how you would act in its place?
If capable open models stay cheap and widely available, who captures the value of AI, and who bears the risk?
What evidence would persuade you that China's stance is a matter of timing and not a different view of the technology?

stories.headline: Late risers who ran the largest empire
stories.dek: Samuel Hughes argues that the Victorian governing class's parties, games and classics were a deliberate machine for producing cohesion and public service.
body: Modern advice on success has a recognisable shape. Rise early, take a cold bath, study something technical and work long hours. Samuel Hughes, an editor at Works in Progress, sets against it the habits of the class that ran Victorian Britain. Its members learned little science, got up late, drank a great deal and spent much of their waking lives at parties.

By their own measures they did rather well. Britain was the richest country on Earth for much of the century. Its firms dominated world trade and its navy the seas. A small army won many wars while governing a vast empire, and the country reformed its way towards democracy without the revolutions that struck the continent. Hughes states plainly that this success rested on the subordination of hundreds of millions of people. His question is narrower: did the elite's relentless investment in soft skills, team-building and networking actually work?
His tentative answer is that it did, and that the example should make anyone hesitate before assuming there is only one way to rule.
## Schools for character

Today's education debates pit traditionalists, who favour knowledge and structure, against progressives, who favour skills and freedom. The surprise in Hughes's account is that elite Victorian schools leaned progressive in several respects.

Boys usually left home at seven or eight for preparatory school and then moved to one of the public schools. Most boarded, so they were raised largely among their peers. Hughes links this to the absence of strong regional loyalties in the British elite, unlike those of the American South, Catalonia or Hungary.

Latin and Greek filled at least half of teaching time. Science was resisted as irrelevant to forming gentlemen; Thomas Arnold of Rugby said he would rather his son believed the sun went round the Earth than have him absorbed in physical science. Most adults forgot their classics, and Hughes thinks the chief benefit was discipline and memory. Classroom hours were modest: about five on a full day at Rugby and two on a half day. Sport, by contrast, took ten to twenty hours a week. One headmaster, Hely Hutchinson Almond, ranked character above physique, intelligence, manners and information.

Prefects held real disciplinary and pastoral power over younger boys. Hughes admits this sometimes turned brutal, and that memoirs make it hard to say how often. But the intention, he argues, was a kind of elite liberalism: training boys to be both subjects and makers of authority.
## Pass men and fast men

Most went on to Oxford or Cambridge, where admission was close to guaranteed. Students could take a demanding honours degree or an easy pass degree. Early in the period most were pass men, and many still were in 1914. Aristocrats in particular preferred rowing, feasting and social polish.

Tutors, often young clergymen holding fellowships as temporary posts, believed a university should form the whole person and not train for a trade; Hughes quotes Benjamin Jowett of Balliol to that effect. Edward Bouverie Pusey dismissed science as mere fact-collecting. Science students took just 8.1% of honours degrees in 1855-60 and 13.7% in 1910-14. Oxbridge did not become a leading research centre, Hughes notes, until scholars fleeing Nazism arrived in the 1930s.

College life ran from chapel through lavish lunches, afternoon sport, tutorials over tea or sherry, debates at the Union and formal dinner. The East India Company's college at Haileybury was similar. Drawing on David Gilmour's account of the memoirs of John Beames, Hughes describes brief lectures and hard-drinking "fast men", and graduates who nonetheless formed lasting bonds. Lord Salisbury valued such friendships precisely because they produced co-operation.
## Breakfast at half past eleven

Adult life kept the pattern. Pitt the Younger breakfasted at nine. Gladstone hosted breakfasts from 10.30 and Disraeli attended them at around 11.30. Arthur Balfour often worked from bed until lunch. Many men spent the morning at home on letters and newspapers before walking to an office in central London. Lunch, substantial by the 1870s, was taken at a club among professional peers. Dinner ran to many courses and much wine; a conduct guide of the time observed that married women often drank five or six glasses.

From February to July came the Season. Most of the elite lived in Mayfair and Belgravia, within walking distance of one another, and Parliament sat in the same months. Balls began at nine or ten, supper appeared around midnight and the best dancing came after one. Unmarried young people might attend three or four a week.

Hughes insists these events were work as well as pleasure. Leonore Davidoff describes them as an information network about jobs, investments and political decisions. Many Victorians were ambitious and overworked. What distinguished them was not idleness but the fusion of social and professional life.
## Method in the madness

To explain why this might have paid, Hughes borrows Ferdinand Tönnies's distinction between Gemeinschaft, community, and Gesellschaft, society. The Victorian elite was a small community sitting on top of a vast impersonal society, bound by shared schooling, shared venues and intermarriage. The arrangement had costs, since hours at balls were hours not spent at a desk. He proposes four benefits.

The first is unity. The elite absorbed Nonconformists, Jews, Catholics and the new urban bourgeoisie, where sectional conflict split the American South, southern Europe and Germany. Ireland is the notable exception. The second is unpaid public service. Until the 1880s local government was run by landowners who received no salary, managed poor relief, sat as magistrates and ran schools and hospitals, and whose standing depended on doing so.

The third is a willingness to pay for the privilege. In the general election of 1880 a candidate's expenses came to about £150,000 in an urban seat and £450,000 in a rural one in today's money, yet competition for seats was fierce. The fourth is restraint. Walter Bagehot claimed that English politicians rarely put party advantage above the national interest. Hughes treats the claim with caution but suggests a shared identity may have curbed divisive politics.
## An untestable thesis

Hughes repeatedly marks the limits of his argument. No controlled experiment can be run on Victorian Britain, so the thesis is hard to test. Bagehot's praise is hard to evaluate. The elite's achievements came at the expense of many of those it ruled. And a model fitted to the nineteenth century may not suit societies whose problems are quite different.

He ends with a thought experiment: a modern city council whose members are Jeff Bezos, Larry Page, Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg. It might be a disaster, he concedes, but it would be an interesting one. The larger point is that the Victorian way of life, so unlike current counsel, was a deliberate system for producing loyalty, networks and public service, and that today's elites may lack some of the strengths it bred.
stories.counterpoint: The simplest objection is that Britain's Victorian success had other causes: coal, an early industrial lead, naval supremacy and a protected island. The elite may have prospered despite its habits, living off advantages it did not create, and its neglect of science is often blamed for the country's later relative decline against Germany and America. Cohesion among a few thousand intermarried families is also another name for a closed shop. Hughes concedes the thesis cannot be tested, which leaves it an attractive story more than a finding.
stories.why: Debates about meritocracy assume that the best rulers are the hardest-working and most technically trained. Hughes offers a counter-example in which trust, shared formation and a sense of obligation did much of the work that credentials are now asked to do. For anyone who builds institutions, from firms to churches, it raises the question of how much effort should go into competence and how much into binding people together.
questions: How much of what your institution achieves depends on trust built outside formal work?
Can a governing class be both cohesive and open to newcomers, or does one erode the other?
What public duties would today's wealthy have to perform for their status to feel earned?

source.title: Why were Victorian elites so effective?
source.author: Samuel Hughes

stories.headline: America has stopped planning for the next century
stories.dek: Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus argue that the contest with China will be decided by which country can still imagine, and build, a long future.
body: America marked its 250th anniversary in 2026 mostly by looking backwards, to the revolution and the founders. Simon Curtis, who teaches international relations at the University of Surrey, and Ian Klaus, founding director of the Carnegie Endowment's California centre, think the retrospection is a symptom. Great powers, they write in Noema, apply their strength over time, and the United States has lost its feel for the future.

Their argument recasts the rivalry with China. The contest is usually described in terms of tariffs, military balances or leadership in frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence and clean energy. Curtis and Klaus say it is better understood as a competition between visions of tomorrow, and between the capacities to build them. On that measure they think America is behind.
The essay is a diagnosis followed by a sketch of a remedy. Both rest on one idea: that power at the scale of a hegemon needs thinking that runs across generations and across borders at once.
## The perpetual present

The cold war, the authors recall, was an intergenerational project. It involved state-guided technological moonshots, the building of a liberal international order and the shaping of cities and infrastructure around the world. That sense of direction faded after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. A run of crises since has left the West without a thread to follow.

They list the clocks that now govern American life. Midterm elections arrive every two years. Administrations last four, and their achievements are reversed by successors. Companies report quarterly, which discourages long investment. News runs on a 24-hour cycle and social media on something far shorter. Drawing on Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity, they describe a culture in which history has become collage and utopian ambition an object of irony.

The Make America Great Again movement, in their reading, is a genuine response to the failed promises of globalisation and to elites who neglected ordinary people. But it is nostalgic. It looks to a vaguely defined past and offers no picture of the future at home or abroad. The unipolar 1990s, when no rival forced the question, were squandered. Two things now expose the malaise: China's rise and climate change.
## A rival that plans in decades

The authors do not judge Americans too harshly. They quote Achille Mbembe, a Cameroonian historian, to the effect that the West as a whole has largely closed off any imagined world to come. Most Western states, moreover, are not great powers even when acting together through the European Union.

China is different. It plans its strategy over decades and is less buffeted by the political and economic turbulence that shapes democracies. Curtis and Klaus cite Rush Doshi, who as a doctoral researcher at Harvard in the mid-2010s reviewed three decades of Chinese-language speeches, party communiqués and military writings and concluded that China had pursued a consistent long-term strategy to weaken and eventually displace American dominance. It was not a sudden turn under Xi Jinping, though it has accelerated under him.

Their main exhibit is the Belt and Road Initiative, built over the past 13 years: ports on the Indian Ocean, rail corridors through Central Asia, fibre-optic cables reaching East Africa, energy transmission and smart cities. The 15th Five-Year Plan, they say, extends state planning to drive investment in technology, infrastructure and supply chains. China's idea of an "ecological civilisation" ties this positioning to the long horizons that climate change demands.
## Invention is not enough

America's two great post-war advantages, the essay argues, were of scale. It linked domestic institutions to international order, as when Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal was woven into the United Nations and the early financial institutions. And it built a network of alliances. The authors think both have been lost, the second through an approach under Donald Trump that treats foreign relations as zero-sum and makes American behaviour hard to predict.

They then turn to technology, citing Jeffrey Ding of George Washington University. Ding argues that great-power technology contests are won by diffusion, the patient work of spreading a technology through society, more than by breakthrough invention. American firms may lead in AI, advanced chips, cloud computing, biotechnology, space launch and quantum computing. But the free-market model for spreading the benefits now faces a state-directed one that diffuses technology at home and reshapes other countries through infrastructure.

The authors note that Silicon Valley's laboratories worry that China's decision to open its AI models to international partners could undercut proprietary American ones. China also controls many critical supply chains, including processed rare earths, batteries and robotics.
## The project-state

For a remedy the authors borrow Charles Maier's concept of the "project-state": a state driven by a historical mission to transform society over a long horizon. Maier, a Harvard historian now in his late 80s, applies the term to Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia as well as to the New Deal, and worries that America has forgotten its own intergenerational mission. The Soviet Union, the authors insist, was not defeated by free markets alone. Washington invested at home and abroad to shape the outcome.

They find materials for renewal in three places. One is the Biden administration, which they partly defend. Its Inflation Reduction Act aimed to drive a green transition, bring jobs to post-industrial regions and restore climate leadership together; Jake Sullivan, then national security adviser, spoke of turning the rust belt into a "cobalt corridor". The effort stalled and was largely reversed. A second is the "abundance agenda" of Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson, with its politics of building. The authors suggest a sovereign Strategic Investment Fund to draw private capital into long projects.

The third is California. Gavin Newsom, its departing governor and a possible presidential candidate in 2028, issued executive orders in May 2026 directing agencies to prepare safety nets for workers displaced by AI. These include subsidies for retraining and an exploration of "universal basic capital", which would give workers a stake in asset funds.
## A railway to Lobito

The essay's closing example is modest. In December 2024 Joe Biden visited Angola to promote the Lobito corridor, a railway linking the Atlantic port of Lobito to the mineral-rich interior of Congo and Zambia. It was part of a G7 infrastructure partnership that borrowed China's methods, ports, corridors and supply-chain security, while leaning on private finance. The change of administration ended the approach.

Curtis and Klaus concede China's weaknesses: an ageing population, heavy debt, a property crisis, little soft power, few allies and a centralised system that could itself become a liability. They do not predict American decline. They describe two paths. On one, American primacy will have lasted about a century, a familiar span. On the other, the country renews its domestic model and ties it to a new international order.

Great powers, they conclude, are judged by the futures they can persuade others to share, more than by wealth or weapons. The question for the next generation of American leaders is whose future their fellow citizens will live in: one they build, or someone else's.
stories.counterpoint: Long horizons are not a virtue in themselves. Maier's own list of project-states includes regimes whose grand designs ended in catastrophe, and China's planners produced the property bubble and the demographic squeeze that the authors mention only in passing. Belt and Road has left bad debts and resentful borrowers as well as railways. America's short cycles are also how it corrects mistakes, and its lead in frontier technology came from firms, not five-year plans. A critic would add that the essay's remedy closely tracks one party's programme.
stories.why: If the authors are right, the things Washington argues about most, tariffs and chip bans, are secondary to whether it can sustain any policy for longer than an electoral term. The claim that diffusion matters more than invention deserves particular attention at a moment when America leads in AI models but lags in building the grids and factories to use them. Allies deciding whose infrastructure to buy are already answering the essay's question.
questions: What is the longest-horizon commitment your own country, firm or church is currently keeping, and who protects it?
Can a democracy plan across generations without weakening the voters' power to change course?
Is a compelling picture of the future something leaders can supply, or does it have to grow from below?

source.title: Americans Are Losing The Long Game
source.author: Simon Curtis & Ian Klaus

stories.headline: India's great service export meets its machine
stories.dek: David Oks traces how India became the world's back office and why AI threatens the labour arbitrage on which the whole industry was built.
body: Poor countries get rich, as a rule, by selling something to rich ones. David Oks, writing in Asterisk's issue on work, runs through the options. Natural resources help but tend to bring overvalued currencies, corruption and weak institutions. Manufacturing lifted East Asia, yet few other poor countries have managed it, and factories need less labour than they once did. That leaves services: selling work down a wire to firms abroad.

India is the great example of the third route. It never built a competitive manufacturing sector; its share of world manufactured exports is about the same as Vietnam's, though its population is 14 times larger. But it is the largest exporter of information-technology and business-process outsourcing services. Oks's essay tells how that happened and then asks what becomes of it now that AI can do much of the same work for less.
His concern is specific. The industry was built on an arbitrage between cheap Indian labour and expensive Western labour. A machine that undercuts both removes the reason for the trade.
## Small sector, large weight

The numbers explain why this matters beyond the firms themselves. Indian IT employs about 5m people in a country of 1.5bn. Yet it produces roughly 7% of GDP and about a quarter of exports. The surplus on services trade was around $190bn in the 2025 fiscal year, which offsets a persistent deficit in goods.

Its workers also matter for what they spend. An IT employee earning about $23,000 a year makes several times India's income per head and buys heavily from domestic services. The matrimonial pages of the Hindu, Oks notes, listed "software engineer" as the most desired occupation. This was never sweatshop labour. The jobs paid well and were keenly sought.
## Born of an exit

The origin story begins with a quarrel. A 1973 law capped foreign ownership of Indian companies at 40%. IBM refused to dilute its stake, the minister George Fernandes held firm, and in June 1978 IBM left, stranding about 800 mainframe installations. Domestic firms filled the gap. Tata Consultancy Services had won its first outsourced contract in 1974, converting accounting code for a hospital in Detroit, on a borrowed second-hand mainframe, with the finished code shipped physically because no data link existed. Infosys and Wipro followed in the 1980s. Wipro had begun as a cooking-oil company. Infosys waited a year for a telephone line and three for a computer.

Two things in the early 1990s turned a cottage trade into an industry. Undersea fibre-optic cables made sending data cheap. And a balance-of-payments crisis in 1991, in which India airlifted gold to London to secure loans, led Manmohan Singh and the prime minister, P.V. Narasimha Rao, to dismantle the Licence Raj and open the economy to foreign investment.
## From Y2K to the peak

Then came the millennium bug, which created huge demand for COBOL programmers, a skill Indian engineers already had. TCS alone fixed about 700m lines of code. Software exports rose from $1bn in 1997 to $6.2bn in 2001, and Infosys listed on NASDAQ in 1999.

Western cost-cutting after the dotcom bust and the financial crisis did the rest. TCS passed $1bn in annual revenue in 2003 and $10bn by 2012. Multinationals set up their own offshore units, the Global Capability Centres, which now number between 1,700 and 2,000 and employ roughly 1.9m people for the likes of JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Google and Microsoft. A General Electric unit started in 1997 with 20 employees had 12,000 within four years. It became Genpact and now employs about 145,000.

By 2021 TCS was valued above $200bn and Infosys at $100bn. In 2022, the peak, TCS added nearly 100,000 staff and Infosys hired 85,000 graduates. Infosys's attrition reached 27.7% late that year, a sign of how fiercely firms were bidding for people.
## The dimming

ChatGPT was launched on November 30th 2022. Doubts followed fast. In February 2023 a J.P. Morgan note called generative AI a deflation driver for legacy IT services. In January 2024 the investor Daniel Gross asked what India's service exports would be worth if they were, in essence, the outputs of an AI model; Oks grants that Gross was being provocative and that early models had obvious limits. India's own 2024 Economic Survey spoke of a huge pall of uncertainty and expected outsourcing employment to fall considerably within a decade. At a summit in India in February 2026 the investor Vinod Khosla predicted that IT services and outsourcing would almost completely disappear within five years.

The labour market has moved first. TCS announced 12,000 lay-offs in July 2025, the largest in the industry's history. Infosys's headcount fell in 2024 for the first time in 22 years, and its graduate intake dropped from 85,000 in 2022 to 12,000. Wipro shed 25,000 jobs over two years. At IIT Delhi the placement rate fell to 61% in 2025, and across 23 IIT campuses about 8,000 students went unplaced, more than double the figure two years earlier. TCS, Cognizant and Infosys have each lost about 30% of their market value in 2026.
## Revenue holds, the pyramid does not

Oks is careful to say that this is not a collapse. Revenue is still growing, though only in low single digits, and headcount is roughly flat. Margins have risen: Infosys's operating margin in 2025 was 21.1%, its best in three years. TCS reports $2.3bn of "AI revenue", much of it implementation work such as building retrieval tools for corporate clients.

What has broken is the labour model. The old firm was a pyramid with a wide base of junior coders. Mohit Joshi, Tech Mahindra's chief executive, now speaks of a "bulging middle". Revenue per employee has climbed to about $50,000 at TCS and $60,000 or more at Infosys and HCLTech. C. Vijayakumar, HCL's boss, said in February 2025 that the company aimed to produce twice the revenue with half the workforce.
## What then?

The essay ends with a downside case that Oks labels a sketch and not a forecast. Western clients need fewer engineers, so export revenue declines. Indian firms, meanwhile, buy AI from abroad by the token, which adds to imports. The balance of payments weakens. Because well-paid IT workers support a large domestic service economy, the contraction spreads.

He allows that the pivot to AI services may keep the firms relevant for some years, and that if AI truly replaces programmers, American ones are exposed too.  For tens of millions of Indians, IT was the path into the global middle class. If it narrows, Oks asks, what then?
stories.counterpoint: Indian IT has been written off before, at the dotcom bust and with the arrival of cloud computing, and each time it moved up the value chain. Oks's own figures show revenue and margins holding, and the hiring slump partly unwinds a pandemic-era binge. Companies everywhere will need help fitting AI into old systems, which is exactly the work these firms sell, and cheaper software has historically created more demand for it. The Global Capability Centres suggest multinationals still want Indian talent, not just Indian prices.
stories.why: India's is the main successful case of development through exported services, and many poorer countries hoped to copy it. If AI closes that route as automation narrowed the manufacturing one, the list of ways for a poor country to grow rich gets shorter. The essay also shows where to look for AI's effect on work: in graduate hiring and the shape of firms well before it appears in revenue.
questions: If revenue holds while hiring collapses, whose interests does a firm's success now serve?
What should a young Indian engineering graduate do differently from one who finished in 2022?
Which path to prosperity remains for poor countries if both factories and back offices need few people?
